title: Unknown Pediatric Ingestion: Stabilize First, Identify the Substance Fast
bottomLine: A child with a suspected unknown ingestion needs immediate ABC assessment, symptom-directed emergency care, and rapid poison-control/toxicology consultation. Do not wait for the exact substance to be identified before treating instability.
recognize: Altered mental status, abnormal breathing, seizures, vomiting, unusual pupils, arrhythmia, or sudden unexplained behavior can signal poisoning.
priorities: Stabilize airway/breathing/circulation, remove ongoing exposure, collect container/history if available, and contact poison experts/emergency services.
assessMonitor: Vital signs, glucose as indicated, neurologic status, respiratory pattern, cardiac rhythm when appropriate, substance/amount/time and co-ingestants.
interventions: Follow substance-specific poison-control/emergency recommendations; preserve packaging or medication lists.
medicationSafety: Do not give empiric antidotes or induce vomiting unless specifically indicated by current toxicology guidance.
teaching: Store medicines and chemicals out of sight and reach and use child-resistant packaging correctly.
delegationScope: Emergency supportive care is immediate; antidote and decontamination decisions require poison-control/provider direction.
examTrap: Delaying ABC support while family members search the home for the missing medication bottle.
oneLinePearl: Poisoned child: stabilize first, identify and consult in parallel.

title: Swallowed Poison: Do Not Induce Vomiting
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Routine induced vomiting and ipecac are not recommended for swallowed poison exposures. Obtain poison-control guidance and treat based on the substance, amount, age, symptoms, and time of exposure.
recognize: Caustic, hydrocarbon, sedative, and other exposures may become more dangerous if vomiting is induced.
priorities: Remove remaining material from the mouth if safe, assess symptoms, and contact Poison Control/emergency care.
assessMonitor: Substance, concentration, amount, time, symptoms, child weight/age, and airway protection.
interventions: Follow current poison-specific first aid rather than home remedies.
medicationSafety: Do not administer ipecac or unapproved neutralizing agents.
teaching: Do not make a child vomit after a poison exposure; get expert guidance.
delegationScope: Telephone advice should route to poison experts/EMS based on symptoms; medication/decontamination decisions are authorized-clinician actions.
examTrap: Giving syrup of ipecac after an unknown household ingestion.
oneLinePearl: For swallowed poison, don't make them vomit—get expert guidance.

title: Medication Poisoning Prevention: Up, Away, Locked, and Measured in mL
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Prevent unintentional pediatric overdoses by storing medications, vitamins, and supplements up and away after every use, securing child-resistant caps, and using standardized milliliter dosing devices for liquid medicines.
recognize: Young children commonly access medicine left on counters, bedside tables, purses, backpacks, or unlocked containers.
priorities: Assess home storage and caregiver dosing technique during teaching.
assessMonitor: Medication list, storage locations, measuring device, multiple caregivers, and duplicate ingredients.
interventions: Teach mL-only measurement with the matching syringe/cup and secure storage even when a child-resistant cap is present.
medicationSafety: Do not use household spoons or call medicine candy.
teaching: Store every medicine and supplement out of sight and reach after every use; keep Poison Help information accessible.
delegationScope: Medication teaching can be reinforced by PN/LVN; dosing prescriptions remain provider/pharmacy directed.
examTrap: Assuming a child-resistant cap makes countertop storage safe.
oneLinePearl: Child-resistant is not child-proof—store medicine up and away every time.

title: Caustic Ingestion: Protect Airway and Avoid Neutralization Experiments
bottomLine: Drooling, oral burns, painful swallowing, vomiting, stridor, or respiratory distress after a caustic product exposure requires urgent airway-focused evaluation. Do not induce vomiting or attempt chemical neutralization.
recognize: Absence of visible mouth burns does not fully exclude deeper injury.
priorities: Assess airway/breathing, keep child from further exposure, and contact poison/emergency specialists immediately.
assessMonitor: Voice/stridor, drooling, swallowing, oral findings, respiratory effort, pain, vomiting, product and concentration.
interventions: Keep NPO as directed and prepare for specialist evaluation/endoscopy according to the care plan.
medicationSafety: Do not give acids/bases to neutralize the product or routine activated charcoal without toxicology direction.
teaching: Keep cleaning products in original locked containers, never beverage bottles.
delegationScope: Airway emergency support is immediate; decontamination/endoscopy decisions are specialist-directed.
examTrap: Trying to neutralize drain cleaner with vinegar or another household product.
oneLinePearl: Caustic ingestion: airway first, no vomiting, no home neutralization.

title: Inhaled Poison: Fresh Air Without Becoming a Second Victim
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: For inhaled toxic fumes, move the child to fresh air only when rescuers can do so safely, avoid entering a contaminated environment without protection, and obtain poison/EMS guidance. Respiratory or neurologic symptoms require emergency evaluation.
recognize: Cough, wheeze, dyspnea, headache, confusion, dizziness, collapse, or multiple ill household members can signal inhalational exposure.
priorities: Scene safety, fresh air, ABC assessment, emergency activation for significant symptoms.
assessMonitor: Oxygenation/respiratory effort, neurologic status, exposure source/duration, co-exposed persons.
interventions: Remove contaminated clothing/decontaminate only as substance-specific guidance directs.
medicationSafety: Oxygen and antidotes are indication/protocol dependent; carbon monoxide severity cannot be judged by conventional pulse oximetry alone.
teaching: Never re-enter a fume-filled space without appropriate rescue protection.
delegationScope: Scene rescue follows EMS/hazmat safety; clinical treatment is provider-directed.
examTrap: Sending a parent back into a contaminated room to retrieve the product label.
oneLinePearl: Fresh air helps only if the rescuer stays safe too.

title: Acetaminophen Exposure: Early Wellness Does Not Exclude Serious Toxicity
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A child may initially look well after a potentially toxic acetaminophen ingestion. Accurate time, product concentration, estimated amount, weight, and prompt poison/emergency evaluation are essential because treatment decisions are time-sensitive.
recognize: Caregiver dosing confusion, multiple acetaminophen-containing products, or missing tablets/liquid can create overdose even without early symptoms.
priorities: Obtain exposure details and escalate promptly rather than waiting for jaundice or severe illness.
assessMonitor: Time/amount/product, weight, vomiting, liver-risk history, and ordered acetaminophen concentration/liver studies.
interventions: Support ordered toxicology evaluation and antidote pathway.
medicationSafety: N-acetylcysteine decisions are protocol/toxicology directed; do not delay evaluation until symptoms develop.
teaching: Check combination cold/flu products for acetaminophen to prevent duplicate dosing.
delegationScope: Exposure-history collection is appropriate; toxic-dose calculation and antidote decisions require poison/provider oversight.
examTrap: Reassuring the family because the child has no symptoms two hours after a possible overdose.
oneLinePearl: Acetaminophen toxicity can be quiet early—history and timing drive action.

title: Iron Ingestion: Severe GI Symptoms Can Precede Systemic Toxicity
bottomLine: Iron-containing prenatal vitamins or supplements can cause dangerous pediatric poisoning. Significant vomiting, abdominal pain, bloody GI symptoms, lethargy, shock, or a credible large ingestion requires urgent toxicology/emergency care.
recognize: Prenatal vitamins are a common high-risk household source because tablets may contain substantial elemental iron.
priorities: Stabilize, identify product/strength/amount/time, and contact poison/emergency experts.
assessMonitor: GI symptoms, perfusion, mental status, metabolic status/labs as ordered, and exposure details.
medicationSafety: Do not assume a vitamin is harmless or administer home antidotes.
teaching: Store prenatal vitamins and supplements like prescription medicines—up and away.
delegationScope: Supportive monitoring is role appropriate; chelation/decontamination decisions are toxicology/provider directed.
examTrap: Calling iron tablets low-risk because they are sold over the counter.
oneLinePearl: In children, iron vitamins can be toxic medicine.

title: Button Battery Ingestion: Time-Critical Esophageal Injury
bottomLine: Suspected button-battery ingestion is time critical because an esophageal battery can rapidly cause severe tissue injury. Arrange immediate emergency evaluation and do not wait for symptoms.
recognize: Unexplained drooling, dysphagia, chest discomfort, vomiting, cough, or a missing battery can be clues, but children may initially be asymptomatic.
priorities: Emergency evaluation with rapid imaging/removal pathway as directed; identify battery type/time if known without delaying care.
assessMonitor: Airway, swallowing, drooling, respiratory symptoms, pain, ingestion time and battery source.
interventions: Keep child on the emergency toxicology/GI pathway; avoid inducing vomiting.
medicationSafety: Do not give unapproved food/drink remedies unless current poison/battery guidance specifically directs them for the child's age and timing.
teaching: Secure batteries in locked compartments and dispose of loose batteries safely.
delegationScope: Emergency recognition is immediate; imaging/removal decisions are specialist led.
examTrap: Observing at home because the child swallowed the battery without choking.
oneLinePearl: Button battery in the esophagus is a clock-running emergency even before symptoms.

title: Childhood Lead Exposure: No Safe Blood Lead Level Has Been Identified
bottomLine: Young children are especially vulnerable to lead from deteriorating pre-1978 paint, contaminated dust/soil/water, imported products, and take-home occupational exposure. Suspected exposure requires provider follow-up and blood lead testing—not reassurance based on absence of symptoms.
recognize: Many exposed children have no obvious acute symptoms; developmental, learning, behavioral, hearing, or growth effects may occur.
priorities: Identify environmental risk and ensure testing/follow-up according to public-health guidance.
assessMonitor: Housing age/renovation, water/plumbing, imported foods/spices/remedies/cosmetics, caregiver jobs/hobbies, pica, developmental concerns.
interventions: Reinforce exposure-source control and public-health/environmental resources.
medicationSafety: Chelation is not a preventive home treatment and is reserved for specific blood levels/clinical circumstances under specialist direction.
redFlags: Neurologic symptoms with possible severe poisoning
teaching: Lead cannot be reliably detected by taste or appearance; prevention focuses on eliminating exposure sources.
delegationScope: Screening history/education can be reinforced; testing interpretation and chelation decisions require provider/public-health oversight.
examTrap: Waiting for neurologic symptoms before recommending testing in a child with a credible exposure.
oneLinePearl: Lead harm can occur without symptoms—risk history should trigger testing, not watchful waiting.
sourceBasis: CDC Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention guidance

title: Poison Exposure Handoff: Substance, Amount, Time, Symptoms, Weight
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: A useful poison-exposure handoff includes the exact product/concentration if known, estimated amount, time, child's weight/age, symptoms, first aid already given, co-ingestants, and poison-control recommendations. Missing these details can delay correct treatment.
recognize: Brand name alone may not reveal concentration or active ingredients.
priorities: Bring the container/photo/label when safe and document poison-control case recommendations accurately.
assessMonitor: Exposure route, product, amount, time, weight, symptoms, interventions and response.
interventions: Use closed-loop handoff between family, poison center, EMS, ED, and inpatient teams.
medicationSafety: Document antidotes/decontamination exactly; avoid duplicate administration during transfers.
teaching: Do not discard the container after an exposure; bring it if safe.
delegationScope: Data collection may be shared; clinical interpretation and treatment decisions are authorized-clinician responsibilities.
examTrap: Handoffing only 'child drank cleaner' without product, amount, time, weight, or symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Poison handoff lives on five anchors: what, how much, when, weight, and symptoms.
